utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Robinson, and I would like to thank the Bench as well. I have stated a portion of my arguments yesterday concerning our position that this document shouldn't be admitted as the Prosecutor seeks to do. I will try to explain the rest of our arguments, trying to be as brief as probable. First of all you made a decision as to whether it is possible to hear another witness here, who is a senior police official by the name of Nedzad Vejzagic. That proposition was rejected by the Bench. I do not wish to go into any arguments as to this at this moment. However, there is another attempt now to do the same thing, something that they tried to do via Mr. Kucanin, who headed a part of the investigations and a group of investigators. It is now being tried to be done through another witness pertaining to a part of the indictment, speaking about the long sniping and shelling campaign. I believe there are 218 files pertaining to specific events, and it is now being attempted to introduce all of those through this witness. I have nothing personally against the witness. He came here to speak about his knowledge of two events of the 1st of July and the 23rd of July, 1995, and we are most likely to hear what he has to say about that. As for the other events, he has no knowledge of them. It is a voluminous material, each file containing 50 or 60 pages. What he could have been able to see were perhaps the dates and times but that's it about it. If we draw a parallel, you know that in another case, this being the Milutinovic et al, there was decision made on the 18th of April, the Bench handed it down. It had to do with accepting numerous reports about situation of human rights in Kosovo and Metohija. That Bench deemed it important to have firsthand information from the spot provided by an independent body and these were NGOs collecting general information. On the list of documents being tendered, there were specific cases stated with the goal of being used in that case in order to prove one of the key points in the indictment. A key point is conducting a long-term sniping and shelling activity and campaign against the civilian population of Sarajevo. There's another thing I wanted to say which I believe to be a key thing in this case. The position of the OTP that there was a systematic and widespread attack on the civilian population causing a great number of victims and that this was the only thing that was of interest to the SRK, that is to target civilians. This is what they base the entire case on. Through this witness who was supposed to testify on but a few incidents, they are trying to prove the most important point in the indictment, and they were unable to do that so far. They tried to prove certain incidents which may have been characteristics and now they are trying to put this witness forward in order to get some alleged arguments to strengthen their thesis about the existence of such a strategy. It cannot be done through this witness. I believe that this attempt by the Prosecutor -- I believe that this attempt by the Prosecutor to try and prove something of fundamental importance for this case, i.e., this is not merely collecting general information. This is no general data. These are documents that had to be testified on by a team leader, a person such as Kucanin. He was the person who put the reports together, who compiled the documents and he was the only person who could explain things to us. If we try to tender these documents through this witness who knows nothing of any of these events, apart from being able to leaf through the 218 incidents and we will yet, I hope, be able to see how much time he needed to see the general nature of the documents and what he was able to extract from it. With Kucanin, one would have needed eight hours to discuss that. In the given situation in context, I can ask no questions of this witness about this topic since he has no knowledge of that, plus we have been allotted a very short time. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to rule against something which would be fundamentally unfair to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. The Chamber will give its ruling on this matter. The Prosecution seeks to admit into evidence a spreadsheet made on the basis of a compilation of police reports on a large number of incidents prepared by several police stations in Sarajevo, including the police station in which the present witness was employed as a crime scene technician. The spreadsheet contains information of the exact time and place of the incidents, the weaponry used, the number of victims, and the alleged origin of fire. The purpose of the document, according to the Prosecution, is to substantiate the widespread nature of the attacks against civilian targets in Sarajevo during the indictment period. This document is sought to be admitted through a witness who did not himself draft any of the reports and whose knowledge of the incidents only extended to the limited number of investigations in which he himself was involved. The authenticity of the reports on the remaining incidents was only confirmed, on second-hand, by another police officer, who told the present witness that the reports were authentic and true. The Trial Chamber is reluctant to admit a document through a witness who has little or no direct relation to most of the reports and who is unable to testify to the substantive information contained in the spreadsheet. If admitted, furthermore, the Defence would have no chance of challenging the spreadsheet's information during its cross-examination of the witness, because the witness would be unable to testify to the veracity of most of the substantive information contained in the spreadsheet, let alone to the reliability of most of the underlying police reports. In the Trial Chamber's view, the spreadsheet could only be used for the purpose of showing that there were a great number of incidents involving an even larger number of victims in Sarajevo reported by the police during the indictment period. The defence would be unable to challenge this information through cross-examination, in particular the information on the alleged origin of fire. The Trial Chamber, therefore, will only admit the spreadsheet for the limited purpose of showing the great number of incidents and victims in Sarajevo reported by the police during the indictment period. Beyond this limitation, the probative value of the spreadsheet would be substantially outweighed in the terms of Rule 89 (D) by the need to ensure a fair trial. Cross-examination of the witness by the Defence on the basis of the spreadsheet will therefore be confined to the matter of the number of incidents and victims thereof reported by the police during the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: At the end of the investigation, what conclusions had you and your colleagues reached as to how many air bombs actually were involved?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded that it actually involved only one aerial bomb, which in our view, ricochetted twice before landing in the final location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And are you aware of an expert report earlier submitted in this trial in which a Professor Zecevic from the University of Sarajevo disagrees and considers that there were in fact two bombs, as you and your colleagues had first thought?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what is your view about the possibility of what Mr. Zecevic says being correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is still a possibility. We made our conclusions based on the very few shrapnel marks and the parts of the bomb as well as rocket boosters found. Or, rather, very little of it was found, much less than one would usually expect to be able to find at the scene of explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you -- the first sentence of your answer, "I believe it is still a possibility," the "it" in that sentence, is that your and your colleagues' conclusion or Professor Zecevic's conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Zecevic's conclusion, his expert conclusion is possible that it actually happened as he think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could please go on now to 65 ter 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There on the right-hand side of the screen, Mr. Turkovic, you see a B/C/S document. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.text: As P604, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, based -- according to these reports, how -- were there casualties from this air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people listed. The people who were at the scene of impact. The two being Enis Kadic and Kemal Mortuza.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, And finally, at the scene, Mr. Turkovic, did you take photographs?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could we please see 65 ter number 54.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. In any event, is what is on the screen a report from the police concerning an air bomb incident on 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is it a report of an incident -- a report of an investigation in which you participated yourself?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could see, please, 65 ter number 02928.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you now is a colour photograph. Do you recognise that as one in the series of photographs which you took?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, according to these reports, were there casualties at the scene of the air bomb incident on the 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then the last couple of questions that I have go back to the spreadsheet that was admitted a couple of minutes ago for a limited purpose. utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are there any times of day that reports or requests are not coming in that are blacked out in terms of calls for help?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I hope that according to the actual situation during my cross-examination and in view of these reports admitted on the part of the Prosecution, I will be given a little more time, although I am almost sure that I will finish within the slot allotted to me. Mr. Turkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tapuskovic, bear in mind the limit the purpose for which the spreadsheet was admitted and that in fact we only admitted them for the purpose of showing the number of incidents and victims. The admission did not go any further than that, so you need not concern yourself about the other matters such as origin of fire and the other data set out in the spreadsheet. And the Chamber's ruling confines cross-examination to the two matters of the number of incidents and the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand very well, Your Honour, Judge Robinson, your ruling and the gist of the ruling, and in that respect I'm going to focus myself on a very limited number of questions regarding this document. You can rest assured that I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turkovic, I represent the accused Dragomir Milosevic and I would like to ask you a number of questions in order to enable the Chamber to evaluate in a valid way your testimony. In front of me I have document 65 ter 02873. It's already been tendered as Exhibit P600. It was admitted yesterday and this is your statement given on the 10th of March. Now, I will like to ask you a few questions about your statement of the 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the document. According to what is written here, can you confirm that this is your statement?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we see my name, it is probably my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And there is your signature?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it, but it is possible -- yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, if we can please bring it up, the first sentence -- or, rather, the next one, which reads: "I went to a technical college in Pofalici and at the age of 18 I went into the JNA for my military training." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, that is in 1990, because it says here that in December you were in Slovenia, wasn't that the time when the situation was normal? It was a normal obligation of every male citizen?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only I went to the army a little bit earlier of my own volition before I was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, since the situation was normal, people from Bosnia-Herzegovina did their service in Slovenia. The people from Slovenia did their service in Macedonia, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I believe the interpreter will soon be asking you to observe the pause between question and answer. Don't overlap. You have to wait until the interpretation is concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you went there and throughout the whole period of your military service, you never felt as a member of an army that was an occupying force in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to the relevance of that question, Your Honour. The case does not concern Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, already in the next sentence the witness mentions the dates 26th or 27th June, 1991, when the conflict broke out there Slovenia and he says: "I was in barracks in Novi Mesto and we were surrounded by Slovenian troops." Everything that subsequently happened in Yugoslavia began in Slovenia on that day. In view of what I just read out to you, Witness, can you say that in the barracks where you were -- and this is the relevance of my question, because the same later happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina when barracks were surrounded, the barracks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Were you surrounded, besieged in the barracks, was there any shooting at the barracks and were there any soldiers who died as a result?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My barrack was not fired at. There were some shots fired at guards in our area of responsibility and it was coupled with certain things that were happening inside the barracks in terms that certain officers turned into some strange creatures. They started singing Chetnik songs and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And while they were singing Chetnik songs, you were under siege and your life was threatened?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our lives were never threatened in the barracks. As I said, most shots were fired at outposts where there were soldiers on guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As we can see from this very short sentence you say: "We were then withdrawn to Serbia." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened a few months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were not sent to any strategic positions around Sarajevo, but the army, rather, withdraw, heading for Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, as far as my unit was concerned. The army withdrew either to Bosnia-Herzegovina or to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it physically possible otherwise then to withdraw the army along these two routes? It couldn't fly over Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to reach other parts of the country. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say, that the ultimate destination of these units was either Serbia or Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say: "I returned to Sarajevo," and you left the army? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I went to see my father who had a surgery and I spent the four days of my leave that had been granted to me in Sarajevo and I never went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you speak about you living in Dobrinja. After that, you moved to Alipasino Polje and then you joined the military police. When did that happen? Whose military police?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the summer of 1992. To tell you the truth, I don't know exactly when that happened. It was the military police of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I can see here, you remained in the police until February, 1993. Can you describe for me your duties as a military policeman. What were you involved in?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you say: "In February, 1993, I went on a course for criminal technicians which was organised by the Ministry of the Interior." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this lasted until June of that year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted six months, probably until June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This course involved certain skills and knowledge relating to police work involved in public security duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a specific course intended for crime scene technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For ordinary crimes like threats, violent crimes and other crimes of that nature?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including -- including fires, explosions and similar occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So among the subjects that you studied, there was a photography course as well, is that correct, examination of the crime scene, examination of fingerprints, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mainly general things relating to traditional crimes?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you had some partial study of ballistics and fire-arms. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. Yes, there was a subject that dealt with these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you resumed your duties in the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you became an investigator of all crimes relating to the army; is that correct? Like black marketeering, property crimes, drug smuggling et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now you say: "In December, 1993 I left the military police and joined the civilian police." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you went on to say: "I worked as a street police officer for a year and then I was transferred to the centre of public security." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, if your answer is affirmative, that if in December, 1993 you joined the civilian police and worked as a street police officer, that since a year later you moved to the Security Services Centre, you became involved in crime scene investigations in December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I don't know whether the month is correct, but it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we see that you -- that your responsibility for -- was for municipality of Ilidza and you worked on all kinds of crimes. How long were you involved in the general crime investigations after December, 1994, because this is what you say here, that you dealt with general crime involving civilians, and I presume by that you mean the citizens of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever there was an on-site investigation of a crime, whether it was something relating to war or general crime, and a crime scene investigator was required on the scene, in Ilidza I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that for a number of months in 1995 you were most times involved in this type of civilian crimes?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say here after you came to work in December: "My area of responsibility was the municipality of Ilidza and I worked all kinds of crimes there. Some of the crime related to general crime involving civilians." Was this predominantly your job at the time?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, this was not the focus. I predominantly had to do with shell incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until end 1994, as we've discussed, you were not with the CSB and you never mentioned in your statement that you had anything to do with shelling?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether in 1995 for a number of months I predominantly had to investigate ordinary crimes. I said no. I said that I usually dealt with shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago you said that until the end of 1994 you mainly worked on civilian crime and then moved to the CSB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will wait for the interpreters. I said I was a beat policeman or a patrolman, whatever the term was that you used, until I don't know exactly what month in 1994, but that is not of the essence. What is is that from that moment on I was a crime scene technician in the municipality of Ilidza, and from that moment on, most of the incidents I investigated had to do with shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will have to ask you something again, something to explain to me. Until December, 1993 you worked where you told us did. For a year you were a beat policeman. I asked you about December, 1994 and I told you -- I put to you that you started working on other tasks as of that month.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that in 1994 I started working as a crime scene technician. I don't know of what month exactly. Everything else is as stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A few questions about the document admitted by the Bench with its limited scope. If we forget about the first incident in May, 1995, could you please go to -- I don't know what the number was that was assigned to this document. It is the list or the spreadsheet 605? No. P602, 602. Let us have a look at a few pages at the beginning of the document. If we look at the dates -- let's forget about May, the first date. But look at -- what you have here is August as the second incident. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then September, 1994. Then again September, 1994, all the way to the bottom of the page. On page 2, or, rather, the next page, it's all September, 1994. We can go to page 3. November, 1994. And then the page after that. December, 1994. The last is at page 5. The 27th of December, 1994. Is that correct? That was page 5.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First you said that you started working on these tasks in December. Let's say the end of that year. As for the incidents before that, throughout 1994, you knew nothing about that by way of information working as a policeman, since you were in the police as a patrolman?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Perhaps I could add something. What I did was confirm that these documents seemed authentic. This is the type of documents that I would conclude came from the police. The rest, it's not something for me to say. I don't know whether these things actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the last two items, the 26th of February and then the 4th of March on page 5. On page 6, the 5th of March, the 12th of March. In total, there are four incidents which took place in these entire five months. Can -- is it fair to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything else to the end is May, June, July, August, September -- well, let's say we go as far as August. It continues until the 30th of August and that was the period of most of the incidents. That is on page 21.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. What I see here is page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 21, please. In any case, can you confirm -- well, I won't go into percentages, but between May and August, the 28th or the 30th of August, according to this document, and provided you leafed through it, and you said you did, there were 80 per cent of all the incidents more or less. Don't hold me to the exact percentage.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't ask me to do any statistics on the spot. So if you say so, I'll take your word for it. I hope you did your math.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can go back to your statement, since I have no further questions as to the spreadsheet. You continue with your statement by saying that you investigated shellings. In 1994, you didn't have to do anything about any sniping incidents and have you no knowledge of such incidents, do you? As a policeman, I mean.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I had any on-site investigations concerning sniping. As a civilian I did encounter such incidents, but as a policeman, I cannot really recall, pertaining to the period you mentioned, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence on page 2, you mention a sniping and you say the following: "I also attended one incident when a civilian was shot by -- from a sniper." It was the only sniping incident that you participated in or attended between 1994 and the end of the war as a crime scene inspector?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Ilidza was not exposed to much sniping, since it was closer to the centre, as opposed to some other parts of Sarajevo, I didn't encounter such incidents frequently. Some of my colleagues who worked in other parts of the city did encounter them on a more frequent basis. I'm not saying that there were none in my part of the city, but far less than in other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on. We have to speed things up. You did those investigations and you said: "My job was to find out with where it came from to examine the traces and come to a conclusion." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was to find traces or marks at the scene, to mark them, and if there is any physical evidence, they had to be sent for further expert analysis, and it was up to me to write a report on the traces and marks found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that your ballistic expertise was very modest at the time?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a need for any ballistic expert opinion, we sent sketches with the position of marks, photographs or -- and descriptions and we would send those to ballistic experts. We didn't go into any such detail as to study ballistic traces, which could eventually or potentially be used as evidence. We only provided a preliminary crime scene technician's opinion, which would then be sent for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, you said -- no. When you went to the army you were 18, and by the end of 1993, if I may say so, you were only 21?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we go the next page, page 3, and in the English it is at the end of page 2 and the top of page 3, the last sentence. You mainly had to do with photography as a member of that team. You were in charge of the camera?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not mainly. It was one of my duties. If there was anyone taking photographs, in 99 per cent of the cases, it was me, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last sentence at page 3, the first paragraph, you say: "Sometimes I had to go to the morgue to photograph corpses." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the cases that you testified to today during the examination-in-chief and pertaining to the events of the 1st and the 23rd of July, in neither of the cases you didn't photograph any victims at the location, and here I particularly have in mind the 23rd of July. Those two women were not on the spot, were they?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something will have to jog my memory, because I think the on-site investigation was carried out a few hours after the incident, not immediately after but a few hours later, and it wasn't realistic to expect that the corpses would be there. I believe you are correct in saying that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you went through all of the documents, as you said, concerning the spreadsheet that was admitted, did you in any incident see any photographs of bodies taken at the spot? If there were fatalities, did you see a single corpse, was it photographed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such cases. One wouldn't reasonably expect that. Most of these people were immediately transported to hospitals, trying to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, that is reasonable to expect and no crime technician would do otherwise. But what such cases -- what happened in such cases when people were obviously dead?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall a single incident in which a person wasn't being helped or people tried to help. They would first take that person to the nearest medical facility to see whether the person was dead indeed or whether there was any chance to resuscitate them. I'm not telling you that there were no incidents of people being killed on the spot, but I simply cannot recall a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As a crime scene inspector, wouldn't you say that that would be one of the basic tasks of such an inspector, to try and establish the existence of fatalities. One doesn't need a medical doctor for that. If you find a corpse, don't you take photographs first as one of the basic tenants of the profession, of ballistics in general, of the science as such?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpreter. This would not be an everyday or routine task. Quite often, the spot was still being shelled when we arrived. Therefore, we would be called by neighbours and they would be the first people to get there, they would be the people transporting the victims to the nearest medical facility. It wouldn't be a regular call when someone would say, well, there was a homicide and then the police would be the first to get there. But first people would try to save victims' lives. It was a wartime situation. It wasn't primary to bring the police to the scene but to try and save lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't dwell on it any further. I understand that, of course, you tried to help a person that was hurt. But in cases when it was clear that someone had been killed, was it necessary to expose your own lives to danger to try and pull out a corpse, putting it before the interests of an investigation, which would be better off with the corpse being left on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, mister --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The witness has already testified that he personally was never at the scene of an incident where a person was so obviously deceased that they could forgo taking the person for medical assistance. So the question just put to the witness implicitly misstates the evidence that the witness has just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, I agree. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now you talk about bombs that landed and that you investigated. In order to save time, I would like first to move on to incident of the 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have brought up Prosecution evidence -- Exhibit P603. Page 2 of the official report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 you can read that you received a report, and a while ago you confirmed that you are aware of this report and that you worked on it. You didn't sign it though?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on this report. Actually, I was involved in this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't visit the scene on that day, that is, on the 1st of July, but in fact you only went there on the 2nd of July. This is what is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But towards the end of paragraph 2 you say: "On the 1st of July, the criminal investigation police inspectors received certain information from the head nurse of the hospital in Hrasnica." Is that correct? That certain individuals sustained serious or light injuries?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that, you say here. I would just like to point out that this is it not my report, but I can confirm that it's written in the report as you have just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's only mention of one person sustaining serious injuries and remained in the hospital. Is that correct? Because this is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find that particular section, but if you read it, then I believe that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the witness of the last name Kadic. We don't have the supporting medical files, but it doesn't say here how this person sustained these injuries, what caused the injuries. Were the injuries caused by debris or by shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 3, and here is a list of people who sustained light injuries. And then the next page. Page 3 in English. Here you can see the list of names, seven or eight, all of them were lightly injured. But there is no description of the nature of the injuries and the cause of the injuries, whether it was from debris or from shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was the cause. I'm just confirming what you have read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we go on, on the same page we can see that on -- you visited the scene on the 2nd of July at 8.00 and that you were among members of the team; is that correct? It says Vekaz Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to read all of it. It says here that you have seen a crater, and in the ground as well, in the close proximity, a few pieces of shrapnel were detected. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at the next page, which is page 4 in English. I am not going to read the whole text to you. There is mention of damage to houses and the huge damage caused. However, there is no mention of a single piece of shrapnel found in any of those houses. You can read it for yourself, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see here is the finding of rocket engines. I don't see any mention of shell fragments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, there is a mention of shell fragments at the end of the first paragraph. It says: "Shell fragments were removed from the site." Do you see that, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what the translation says. Except rocket engines that have been found, there is no mention of any pieces of shrapnel being recovered. The only pieces found were in the ground. There is no mention here of shrapnel. The only mentioned here is what Mr. Turkovic himself has found, and that is that rockets' engines were recovered and it is clearly stated in the B/C/S version. I allowed the witness to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would not shell fragments qualify as shrapnel? Because the text which is in English has a reference to shell fragments. I brought that to your attention earlier. The last sentence at the end of the first paragraph: "Shell fragments were removed from the site."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Maybe we should request the translator, interpreters to read the text in the B/C/S and to tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would the interpreters please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is not a single pieces of shrapnel and the witness confirmed that there is only rocket engine, there is no shrapnel, absolutely not a single one. What I read earlier, some shrapnel were found in the hole where the crater was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I asked the interpreters to do something. Why did you interrupt? Would the interpreters -- would you please bring the page back up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The last part of the sentence of the second paragraph on page -- I don't know which page in B/C/S. It's on the screen now -- reads as follows literally: "Whereas parts or pieces of the aforementioned projectile were recovered on the scene."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Maybe we can start here, the UN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, would -- Would you start from the sentence beginning: "The UN Military Observers." It's just the sentence before the last one which the interpreter just translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In front of the house owned by Hamdija Kadic and in the presence of UN military observers, Frank Melum of Norway and Brurmijn of the Netherlands, criminal investigation inspection of the damaged vehicles were carried out, which -- damaged UN vehicles were carried out which sustained total damage. The vehicle in question were Toyota, registration plate number UN, illegible, 6351 and Toyota, registration plate UN PP 15927. The scene and all the recovered physical evidence were fixed by means of measurement, photography, whereas parts of the aforementioned projectile were recovered from the scene."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The English text had "shell fragments." Now we have "parts of the projectile." But move on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to make this clearer--

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you continued on the following day the other location because there was mention there of one or two shell, and it's a continuation of this same document, you speak about the damage. You also speak about pieces of rocket engines that were found and at the end, and that is why I am insisting on this. Before the last sentence it says that: "All the aforementioned traces were secured, i.e., measured and photographed. Parts of the rocket engine were removed from the site." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here in the second part of your investigation, you didn't find-- find a single piece of shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain. Since in a situation like this, there's normally a few thousand pieces of shrapnel, we did not mark every single trace or piece of physical evidence, as would be the standard police procedure. Instead, we only took such number of pieces that would be sufficient for the purpose, and that is what we collected in order to facilitate a subsequent examination of the type of the weapon, because it was simply impossible to retrieve all the pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I showed you what is clearly written on page 2, and it says that in the close proximity of the crater you found several pieces of shrapnel of different sizes and shapes, and you never again mentioned any shrapnel. I'm not expecting you to collect thousands of pieces of shrapnel. You didn't mention a single piece of shrapnel in these houses. You just say that these houses were mentioned. How do you explain that -- damaged? Why didn't you collect also pieces of shrapnel from the location that sustained such heavy damage?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I said before. Standard procedure at the time was to find at least one piece of shrapnel in order to serve as a basis for determining the type of the weapon. The physical evidence that you are referring to, we didn't believe to be necessary. We didn't think it was necessary to collect them, because we -- in each incident we had an enormous amount of physical evidence, and we followed the instructions that we received, and that is to retrieve at least one piece of shrapnel, which would serve as a basis for establishing the type of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not in your pictures at all. However, I'm going to move on to another incident where we have the same situation. It happened on the 23rd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we can please have Exhibit P 608 displayed on the screen. It's 65 ter P 608, it's another report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this report, if you look at it, there is not a single mention of any shrapnel. You also describe huge damage inflicted on the houses and you say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate the paragraph that is he reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreter is asking that you indicate the paragraph that are you now reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's approximately a little bit below the middle of page 1 where Bijelasnicka number 44 street is mentioned. "Where Hasa Rastoder's family house is located, on the top floor of the house in the children's room parts of the missile's rocket motor were found." And then on the next page, Witness, it says under item 6: "Physical evidence recovered." Item 6 reads literally as follows under (a): "Parts of the rocket motors of the missile were found on the first floor of the house in Bijelasnicka street number 44. They were described, photographed and sketched and sent for expert analysis." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned there that photographs were taken, sketches were made, but there's not a single mention of a single piece of shrapnel that could have been taken for expert analysis so as to try and establish what the type of projectile was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEKAZ TURKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At this stage we'll take the break. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no reason to take up any more of your time, and I would like to thank Mr. Turkovic. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the next witness is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be taken by Ms. Edgerton. And may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll begin by going through Mr. Bell's curriculum vitae, and I have spoken to my learned friend in this regard. I will be leading him through his curriculum vitae in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you have been employed with the BBC from 1962 to 1997, I understand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that capacity, you have worked largely as a foreign affairs war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Since what time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Since 1966, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And during the course of those 29, 31 years, you have reported from, I understand, approximately 90 countries and 11 wars or revolutions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The number has since gone up to 100 countries and 15 war zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And among the conflicts you reported from, we can include the Vietnam war in 1968 and 1972; the Arab/Israeli war; Angola in 1976; Rhodesia in 1972; El Salvador in 1983 to 1985; The Gulf War in 1991; as well as events in Croatia that same year. Is my list accurate, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not comprehensive, but it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And from events in Croatia in 1991, am I correct in my understanding that you moved to cover the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you reported on events in Bosnia from the outbreak of war in 1992 to the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: And the implementation of the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Following your departure from the BBC in 1997 you entered politics, I understand, and eventually became the first elected independent member of the British parliament since 1951.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In 2001 you were appointed UK ambassador for UNICEF for humanitarian emergencies, and in that capacity I understand you visited a number of humanitarian and natural disaster scenes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Including Tajekestan in 2001, Malawi in 2002, Iraq in 2003, Darfur the following year, Sri Lanka in 2005, and in 2006 the Congo, Afghanistan and Kabul; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've written three books, one of which In Harm's Way, I understand touched upon your experiences during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including events in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. That book was mostly about the war in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you recently returned to Sarajevo, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. In the unlikely capacity as a travel writer. I went on the first British Airways direct flight from London to Sarajevo and wrote about it and about the country, which I love, with great enthusiasm for the London Daily Telegraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was that most recent visit?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That was at the end the March, just a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could take you back for the rest of your testimony to the period between 1992 and 1995, I'd like to ask you, during your assignments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where did you report from?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I reported initially from a base in the Hotel -- when I started, it was the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo. When the war began we moved to the Hotel Serbia in Ilidza. We went back to the Holiday Inn. We moved out to Central Bosnia to report the side war between Muslims and Croats from mostly from Vitez and Gornji Vakuf. I also travelled extensively throughout the country, including Mostar, Dubrovnik and -- Mostar and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did your reports from Bosnia and Herzegovina include events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that over the three and a half years probably more than half of my reports were about events in and immediately around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mentioned that for various periods of time of you were based at the Holiday Inn. Could you tell us, was the Holiday Inn exposed to Bosnian-Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was very much a front line hotel. It was, I guess, within a couple of hundred metres of the front line for the three and a half years of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was it targeted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. The south side of the Hotel was not demolished but badly damaged by shell fire, cannon fire and mortar fire, so that it was uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, how early did you actually begin reporting from Sarajevo after hostilities broke out?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I started reporting before hostilities broke out in the referendum in March 1992 and after the start of hostilities, and the war was slow to start for reasons we understand. I was there, I suppose, within two days. I must have arrived about maybe the 7th or 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, throughout your time in Sarajevo, did you notice any features of the military activity in and around the city that were unique to that conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that all of the conflicts I have reported, this was the only one conducted continuously and intensively in a modern industrial city and in an urban environment. And of all of the conflicts I have reported, I would say there was the least distinction between soldiers and civilians when it came to targeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So based on what you've just said, then, let me ask you this: Did you observe targeting of civilians in Bosnian and Muslim-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I observed the casualties that occurred among civilians in the -- in the Bosnian government-held side of the city and which I feel would not have happened if there had been any distinction made between military and civilian casualties, but I also believe that civilians were targeted on the Serb side of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we'll explore several aspects of what you said, but perhaps I could first of all pinpoint your observation in time. From what point in time did you observe that casualties occurred among civilians in the Bosnian government-held side of the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would say not immediately, not in the very first few days. The first few days were very confusing days of street fighting between armies and militias and even gangs in which the two sides were trying to establish control in contested territory. But once the lines had solidified, and I would put that around mid-May 1992, it soon became apparent that the greater number of casualties were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make any observations as to the cause of the greatest number of -- of that number of casualties, of the civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. At that phase of the war they were casualties mostly to small arms and sniper fire, to shell fire, to mortars. I had a friend who lived in the old city whose husband was killed in the earlier days of the war by a mortar fired into their house in an old caravanserai near the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did this phenomenon of the firing of sniper fire and shell fire, mortar fire into the cities, into Sarajevo, continue as the war went on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. It was a feature of the entire war, not at a constant level. It came and went. There tended to be a quieter period around mid-winter. Summer was always the worst, and the periods of the most intensive fighting and the highest casualties were the summers of 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did the character of these attacks you have been describing change in any regard as the war went on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. There were different weapons among the weapons employed towards the end of the war. In the summer of 1995, there were serious attempts by the government forces both to break the siege from the inside and break the siege from the outside. That is to say, there was also -- as well as the attacks on civilians, there was a conflict going on between two armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned there were different weapons among the weapons employed towards the end of the war. I'd like to ask you about that. What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The three that we noted that were new, there was a use of a wire-guided missile. There was a use of aircraft bombs rocket propelled into the city of -- of Sarajevo, and on one occasion there was phosphorus.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's your knowledge of who employed or which faction employed these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There was from the start an asymmetry in the forces, that is that the government side had a superiority in sheer manpower but the Bosnian Serb side had a dominance in fire-power, and these new weapons were fired, so far as we could tell, from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to move now to another component of -- or another theme in your testimony in chief and ask you some questions about sniping, which you've already referred to. Do you recall any particularly dangerous areas of the city of Sarajevo in terms of civilian casualties? And in this case I'm referring to Bosnian -- Muslim or Bosnian government-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- because it attempted to be a functioning city, people mostly lived on the west side, and insofar as they had jobs, they worked on the -- in the centre, there were two areas which were -- that were particularly vulnerable. One was what we called "Snipers Alley" near the city hall, and the other was the area outside the Holiday Inn roughly between the Holiday Inn and the museum.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps now I could ask Ms. Bosnjakovic to play clip 1 from the compilation of videos we've prepared for this occasion. And hopefully you'll see it on the screen in front of you in a few seconds, Mr. Bell, and I'll ask you, based on the answers you've just given to have a look at this clip, and I will have some further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, do you recognise on the screen in front of you the location as being either of the two vulnerable locations you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Most, if not all of these pictures appear to come from the first of the two locations to which I referred.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do they bear any resemblance to how you recall those intersections in the early stages of the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: If there is a difference, you can see in the last sequence one of the containers which were put in place to try and protect the people from the snipers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these last clips showed an area that you've spoke about near the city centre. And I'd like to know, did you have occasion to observe sniping activities in the Bosnian government-held areas in the western part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I occasionally and at some risk visited Dobrinja, and I -- and Mojmilo, and there was -- it was not as if the casualties were confined to just these two places. There were very few places except inside the tunnels and the cave down by the Miljacka river which I would say were entirely safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the areas in the western part of the city then, did you ever make observations as to whether sniping or shelling affected conditions of life for the civilians there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, of course they did. You couldn't get into Dobrinja except at risk to your life, because the -- the road in was often under fire. And I remember once in January, 1993 David Owen, the negotiator, driving in with his motorcade and right past the body of a young women who had been killed that night. She had blood on her face, and there was no safe place in that city at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, then, Ms. Bosnjakovic to play clip 2 of the video compilation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to comment, Mr. Bell, on the image of the man climbing out of a window that you've seen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. In many places in Bosnia, not only in Sarajevo, the civilians established sort of rat runs where they could get from one place to another -- place to another, trying to avoid what happened there, because usually it was un -- or often it was unsafe to go out of your front door. That apply to the Holiday Inn as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I move on now to another area, I would ask that the two first clips be admitted as exhibits, please, separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton, could you please tell me when this video was made. Do you have the date of this video?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The second video, Your Honours, or the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Both, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, both videos date from different periods of time because they represent a compilation, but no later than 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these will be admitted as P609 and P610.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, with respect to these two videos which you've noted depicted conditions as you saw them in the early parts of the war, to your knowledge and based on observations, are you able to tell us whether these same conditions existed through 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was not there in the whole of 1994. I was there for most of 1995. I would say that the -- the level of sniper fire and general peril rose and fell. It wasn't constant for three and a half years. The summer of 1992 and 1995 were the worst. It abated considerably and for a while almost to nothing after the cease-fire negotiated by former President Jimmy Carter in December 19 -- Christmas cease-fire, Christmas, 1994, but came back up again about March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've moved on, actually, to 1994, I'd like to ask you whether you're aware of the anti-sniping agreement which was executed in August of that year.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I am. But I think it followed a particularly dreadful incident in which a 11-year-old girl was killed by a shot that ricochetted off the street. And it was -- for some reason the scene was near one of the army headquarters and the camera man had gone there to apply to get permission for something when it happened, so there was very vivid and distressing coverage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall where that 11-year-old girl might have fallen victim? Was it in Bosnian government-held territory or Bosnian Serb-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was in Bosnian government-held territory, very close to the office of the army corps that controlled Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, then, Mr. Registrar, that the document bearing the 65 ter number 1956 be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have it on the screen in front of you, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I've only got what looks like a title, 17 patrol reports, general incidents. I don't have the body of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't even have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't either, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll keep trying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see it now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I only have the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd ask Mr. Registrar to move --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Now -- now --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- to page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Now I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I'd ask you to have a look at this document and the details of the sniping incident dated 11 August 1994 contained therein, and ask you whether that appears, to your knowledge, to be a report on the incident you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have that entered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P611, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, were you able to give numbers to the first two video clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The first video was P609 and the second video was P610.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that following -- you've mentioned that sniping abated following a cease-fire in December 1994 but went on to increase after that. So perhaps I could ask you this, Mr. Bell: Into 1995, what was the safety and security situation in Bosnian government-held territory, in your observation, in terms of sniping? Let's say, in fact, in that period prior to the signing of the cease-fire agreement from November 1994 into early 1995.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was still precarious and remained precarious but not as bad as it had been in the summer of 1992 or as it later became following March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you file reports on the safety and security situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I filed reports on a variety of attacks that occurred on civilians on transportation and really -- and incidents that occurred in "Snipers Alley."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask Ms. Bosnjakovic then if she could play clip 6.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll note, Your Honours, that you see the date that the video was from on the line in the top part of the screen, 24 November 1994. Would you be able to begin the video again, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we stop the video for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, the image --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, the image that we've just seen, an UNPROFOR APC sheltering a group of people, walking slowly beside it, can you comment on that image?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: When I first saw it, I found it very striking. And I haven't seen it again until now. I think it's one of the iconic images of the war. The French were trying to bring confidence to the people and a degree of security down there. That was the area near the Holiday Inn. They instituted this idea of the slowly moving armoured vehicle with the people sheltering. And I think it conveys probably more than any single sniping incident the daily perils of the people in the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we continue, please, now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, are those reports that you filed on the safety and security situation in Sarajevo between November, 1994 and March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would ask Your Honours that these videos on clip 6 be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P612, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ms. Bosnjakovic, would you be able to play clip 5 now for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, do you recognise the locations depicted in this video?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. The location appears to be the -- the second of the two areas that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You can stop the video now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you spoke in respect of the image of the slow-moving APC sheltering people in the previous video, and I wonder in that regard -- as a measure of the protection that UNPROFOR was trying to deliver to the population, I wonder in that regard if can you comment on what you've just seen in clip 5?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. The UNPROFOR was must criticised by the press at the time for not living up to its title and protecting the people. Here it was trying to protect the people and in the second of those two clips, as you can see, it was tragically failing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask this clip 5 be entered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P613, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you're in Sarajevo over the course of long bouts of time between 1992 and 1995, and I wonder if from that perspective you could tell us whether there was any significance to the operation of the trams in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo was in some respect an Austro-Hungarian city and the trams sort of dated from that time, and they were symbolic of the normal functioning of the city. They were stopped, to the best of my recollection, in a big battle on the 2nd of May, 1992, and were -- did not resume for more than a year and a half, I think, till February or March, 1994. And the hope was or the thought was that when the trams resumed, then things were getting better and the UN was doing its job and there was hope for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the trams resumed operation in 1994. Do you recall then following that time the trams having been subject to sniper fire from Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Whether or not they were targeted, they were certainly hit, and I can only surmise they were attractive targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not in terms of the operation or targeting of the trams or the hitting of the trams there was any location at which the trams were particularly vulnerable?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Really, just the same two locations I identified before, but they were most vulnerable, I would have thought, passing that open ground close to the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we turn then to clip 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did I make any reports on these incidents, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that one of your reports, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have that admitted as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, over the course of your work in Sarajevo in particular, do you recall or were you aware of any incidents of UNPROFOR being targeted by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. The detachment of UNPROFOR with area of responsibility in the city centre were the French. The French lost 70 men over the war and some of whom were apparently targeted in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is -- in regard to targeting of UNPROFOR, is there any incident that sticks out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. There was one fairly notorious incident in which a French army engineer was trying to move an anti-sniper block and he was in his vehicle, in his cab, and he was shot and killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall where that took place?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that is in the same place where you have seen most of the French armoured vehicles on the other clips, that is to say, close to the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ms. Bosnjakovic, could you play clip 4 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, does that appear to be the incident that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have that entered as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P615, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were UNPROFOR targeted throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Like the fighting in Sarajevo, Ms. Edgerton, it fluctuated. There were UNPROFOR soldiers killed not only in Sarajevo but in Gornji Vakuf, in the Spanish-held area and elsewhere. Yes, UNPROFOR, throughout the conflict and throughout the country, the casualties they took were not negligible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in Sarajevo in particular, what was the situation as regards the targeting of UNPROFOR in late 1994 and early 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
