utterances.text: The Christmas cease-fire negotiated by Jimmy Carter certainly improved things for a while and a sort of dialogue resumed, but it was mid-winter when it was always easier to establish a cease-fire, and to the best of my recollection, by March 1995 that had started to fall apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you made --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you made reports or broadcasts on the targeting of UNPROFOR at this time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe I did, but I don't have total recall of hundreds and hundreds of reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours, we will play one further clip. In fact, about 15 seconds of your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which number is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It will be clip number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, are these two of your reports that include references to the targeting of UNPROFOR at this time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, they are. I think I said apparently in the first instance. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this clip 3 entered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P616, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, at the outset of your testimony, you mentioned reference to Serb-held areas around Sarajevo. I think in particular Grbavica. And I'd like to ask you: Generally speaking, did you have access to Serb-held areas around the city during the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We began being based in the Hotel Serbia in Ilidza and Ilidza was Serb-held. We continued to have access, rather dangerously, to Serb-held areas. I used to visit Grbavica. When I -- even I was based in Vitez, we regularly went up the mountain road to Pale so it wasn't continuous access, but we had access from the start of the war until August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from that time, was access closed to you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Access was closed the day after the Bosnian Serb referendum on the contact group plan which the Bosnian Serbs rejected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the area of Grbavica, did you observe sniping to have been a concern for the civilians there as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was a concern for the civilians. Of course, there were fewer civilians in these Serb-held areas, because they had the means of getting out of a war zone, certainly if they were not men of military age, but there was anger and deep anxiety about the -- the sniper activity. And I think I wrote in one of my books that there was no monopoly of suffering, and that certainly applies -- applied to the Serbs. And I have been on the receiving end of a Serb sniper myself and I was very lucky to escape. Never -- I beg your pardon. I must change that. I was on the receiving end of a sniper from the Bosnian government side and I was very lucky to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was that, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That was on the balcony in the Hotel Serbia in -- on I would say the 2nd of May, 1992. I was doing a report to London, and I don't know if I was targeted, but we saw later on the recording the bullet coming in at head height, and I dug it out of the wall and put it my pocket as a lucky charm until I was mortared three months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say -- I'll ask you two questions based on what you've said there. Could you tell us exactly where the Hotel Serbia is located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Hotel Serbia is in park land in Ilidza. I believe it the Hotel with the archduke stayed before his assassination. It's a hotel with history very firmly in the Serb-held area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you were mortared three months later. Exactly when was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That was on the 26th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was investigating an outbreak of fighting near the Marsal Tito barracks. I elected to go by the back road. My field craft failed me. I stayed out of the armoured vehicle for too long, and I was hit by -- in the lower abdomen by some mortar fragments.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any information or any opinion as to where the mortar fragments that injured you were fired from or came from?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: You never know for sure, Ms. Edgerton, but common sense tells me that if I'm hit and I am in the government-held areas, I am being targeted or hit by a Serb shell, just as if I'm in a -- with the Serbs and a bullet comes in and nearly kills me, I'm pretty sure it's coming from the Bosnian government side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, going back to the access to Serb-held areas. I would like to ask you, did you ever visit the front lines surrounding Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We were certainly initially made welcome and this happened almost immediately, and Dr. Karadzic, the president of the entity, was happy to show us around.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask Ms. Bosnjakovic then if we could turn to clip number 10, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgive me, Your Honour, but we can't see the picture very well. That might have something to do with the lighting. We can't see what's going on. We just see something moving. We don't see the details. I don't know if anything can be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will ask the technical people to attend to that. Are we able to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. I will just try another time. If it doesn't succeed, a technician has been called. The position is the same? If the position is the same, Ms. Edgerton, move on to another topic and we will return to this. Oh, it's there now. It's there good now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, is that your voice we hear and is that your video report of the visit to the front line?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question, on my colleague and I taking another look at the video, is -- and perhaps you could guide us on this, Mr. Bell. Is this actually a front line location or is it a location that lays behind the front line? And if it assists you, we could play the video again.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. I think I can help you with that. As a general feature of the Bosnian war there were no fall-back positions in trenches. I would say that was one of the Trebinje positions, the one not absolutely closest to the city centre but there was a side road with many more positions like that on it, and that was closer to Pale and it was where Karadzic liked to take us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there -- at this location was there a sniper position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Over the course of your time reporting from Sarajevo and while you had access to Bosnian Serb-held territory, did you ever visit other sniper positions above the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the positions I visited were on the high road to Pale, but in January, 1993, I visited an artillery position north-west of Pale looking right down the Miljacka valley into the city where the Bosnian Serb army had two batteries of what they called mountain guns. These were 100-millimetre artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of this January 1993 visit you've just mentioned, on the compass with the city of Sarajevo at the centre, would you say the artillery positions lay to the north, south, east, or west of the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: These particular positions were to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you give even a rough estimate of approximately how far to the east they lay?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would have thought about ten kilometres, at the most, but closer to the -- obviously, to the front lines, which were very close to them, because the week before we showed up there, there had been an attempt to overrun them by the government forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this location, did you observe a line of sight into the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They had a line of sight, certainly. But they were shooting at the time apparently with cannon fire using tracer on to a government forces front line by a forest, I suppose it was about a kilometre and a half away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the sight was operational at the time you visited?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The artillery pieces were not firing, and the colonel told us he had no intention of firing. Then his line was very similar to that taken in the clip you saw from Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just go back to your answer in the previous paragraph. You say: "They were shooting at the time apparently with cannon fire, using tracers." So I actually took from that, Mr. Bell, that the sight was operational.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Oh, it was an active sight. But in -- in the army, you will seldom have an artillery position with no other defence around it. I said apparently cannon, because we couldn't see the cannon. They were in another part of the same front line giving supporting fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of your reporting from Sarajevo, did you observe that the civilians in Bosnian government-held territory suffered from privations in any regard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, in many regards. There was -- the siege was almost total. There were shortage and -- except to the extent that it was broken by relief flights by the UNHCR, there were shortages of food, of water, of power, both gas and electricity, for much of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see what people did then for fuel, for gas or electricity? How did they cook or how did they keep warm?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They cut down trees, Ms. Edgerton. You will -- if you go to Sarajevo to this day in the city centre you will find very few mature trees except in the park land outside the Presidency. Those were taken for fuel. And as for water, people went to the few water points that were available when the fighting was at its fiercest, and these, of course, included scooping water out of the river itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to your observation did these privations endure throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Like the fighting, they fluctuated. There was a period, there were periods during winter lulls, during cease-fires, during temporary agreements where gas and electricity were intermittently restored. There was a period when the food situation got better, but come April, 1995, the plight of the civilians inside Sarajevo was as desperate as it had been at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, before I move to the next clip, could I tender clip 10, the video of Karadzic, as an exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And ask Ms. Bosnjakovic if she could play clip 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, having looked at these video clips, do they reflect the privations you have described and the way civilians coped through those privations, as you've set out in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. They were obviously shot at different times but -- and in different seasons, but I think they convey the difficulties the population were facing quite vividly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These gatherings of people, as you saw on the first clip, to get water seem to have substantial numbers of people. Do you recall any instance or any information of -- that you might personally have of a water line having been targeted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. It happened near the old maternity hospital. Again it was January, 1993. There was one standpipe from which people could get water, but they were sniped at on their way there. And while we were filming there, one of the water carriers was hit in the leg, so we just stopped work, and my interpreter who was a nurse patched him, and I had the only vehicle, so I took him to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move on, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions relating to shelling and some of the comments you made earlier in your testimony about shelling. Did you observe destruction in Bosnian government-held territory, destruction of buildings caused by the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. You could see it in some of the landmark buildings like the parliament office buildings, the south side of the Holiday Inn, the old library that was destroyed. There was a certain amount of destruction there caused by tank fire, artillery fire and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask clip 12 be tendered as the next exhibit. And we play clip 14 following that. Clip, 12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P618, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now moving on to clip 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've spoken about landmark buildings, Mr. Bell. Do you recognise the building that's burning in the picture in front you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This one, of course, is the parliament office building. The one before were the Unis towers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the next building bearing the flag of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That may have been a Red Cross building. I can't tell. This is a main residential centre, and as you can see, the damage is not caused by small arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have clip 14 tendered as the next exhibit, please. Or could I tender clip 14 as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony, Mr. Bell, you mentioned later in the war Serb used weapons they hadn't used before and you specifically referred to wire-guided missiles, phosphorous and air bombs. If I could refer to the wire-guided missiles first, did you make any report on the use of those missiles?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in an attack on the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask clip 15 be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that your report, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this clip 15 please be marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, next, Mr. Bell, you've mentioned the use of air bombs. What was the first instance in which you became aware of their use; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. It was in Hrasnica very much in the west of the government-held area in the first week of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make a report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Actually, I had difficulty getting the attention of the BBC to allow me to do so, because they said not another explosion in Sarajevo. I said this is different and you should take note of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And why was it different?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was different because this was the first use, to my knowledge, of an aircraft bomb rocket propelled into Sarajevo. This is a -- I suppose we might now call it a weapon of mass destruction, and it is by its nature. We might even call it a weapon of shock and awe. It is so destructive that it is, more than most, incapable of distinguishing between targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we play clip 16, please, and, Your Honours, that relates to scheduled shelling, I think it's number 6 from the 7th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, is that your report on the use of the air bomb in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I note the date of the report appeared inscribed on the top of the video, and it wasn't in fact a report on an incident in June, 1995, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. I remember it as having been in June, but in that case I misremembered. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have this clip 16 marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you aware of the use of air bombs on any other occasion Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. A similar bomb was fired at the television station I believe in July, and it fell in one of the two wells surrounded by big building blocks there and exploded, causing extensive damage and some casualties and an air bomb was also used on a -- it certainly hit a UN vehicle depot close to the television station at about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was this the first time the television station had been targeted with anything?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not at all, Ms. Edgerton. It had been a regular target for attack from the early days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any view as to the appropriateness of the use of this weapon in an urban environment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it is disproportionate and thus against the -- against the rules of law. It has no chance of distinguishing between targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make any observations or come across any information to the effect that the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian government forces had any weapons of the same or similar nature or calibre as these bombs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. They were always short of heavy weapons and they certainly had no rocket-delivered air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also now in terms of different weapons talked about the use of phosphorus. When was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. It was on the 24th of May, 1995. It was identified for us as a phosphorous bomb by the UN spokesman, Colonel Gary Kalet [phoen], who used to be a gunner with expert knowledge of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was the situation in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The situation was -- was very tense. The -- the UN commander, General Smith, delivered an ultimatum to Pale to the Bosnian Serbs on that day. And it -- it ended the following day or the day after with hostage taking of the UN by the Bosnian Serbs or it didn't end there, but it continued with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Over the course of time, you having been in and out of Sarajevo for more or less the -- over the 44 months of the hostilities could you or did you see any effect on the civilian population as a result of the shelling or the sniping or the lack that you've spoken about of basic necessities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. The effects were severe on civilians on both sides of the front lines but especially acute on the government side, because the civilians there had no prospect of escaping. They looked hagard, they looked hunted. Their only business of the day was to get through the day to survive. Survival was what it was about. They were -- they were truly desperate times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, were you in Sarajevo on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make any reports on the shelling of the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please play clip 18 then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this your report, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm -- to this day I'm not happy about it, but because of the BBC's guidelines we were allowed to show very little of the real bloodshed for fear of upsetting people, and I think we took it much too far. The real scenes of what happened there, I wasn't allowed to show, and I think the BBC should be ashamed of itself for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you visit the scene, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Of course, yes. That's my business. It was my business. And as you prepared this report on the incident and its aftermath, did you also have occasion to view film by other agencies?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We ran a pool. It was a cooperative effort, and we had access to all the video that was shot, including the most vivid pictures, which were not included in my television report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could have I this clip 18, please, tendered -- or admitted as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could I ask that clip 19 please be played.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, do you have any comment on the film clip you've just seen, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it's one of the most shocking of the war. On many occasions, and that was one of them, I was thinking to myself that if you ever tried to make a movie of this war, you couldn't. The scenes going on around me could not be replicated for a movie. They were so terrible and they were real world and really shocking, and I also felt this cannot go on. We were more than three years into it. And I said to myself, you know, this cannot go on. It has to be stopped in the name of our common humanity. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have this clip 19 tendered as the last exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P623, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have one last question for you, Mr. Bell. Over the course of your time in Sarajevo reporting from that city in respect of this or any other incident, did you make any observations of Bosnian government forces either firing on themselves or staging incidents?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, I did not, nor of the Serbs or the Croats, either. As I've just indicated, something like that is just -- is just not stageable. On the larger political question, I think that the government forces had a -- and I've said so, in my testimony and in the book I wrote, had an interest in trying to -- to break the siege and they had an interest in attracting the sympathy of the outside world and indeed the intervention of the outside world, but I have no evidence whatever that they would fire on their own people to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear stories to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- Your Honour, there were-- the place was so full of stories. General Lew MacKenzie, when he left in the high summer of 1992, he gave a press conference to the local press in which he said something like, it would help if both sides stopped targeting their own people, and that was left hanging in the air. I've found nothing to corroborate that on -- I mean, I reported this war from, I suppose, all three sides, and I mean, there were armies with an interest in keeping the fighting going. I mean, you've got to be motivated to be a soldier, but I found, myself, no evidence of that. You saw in that last clip the French army engineers were on the spot almost immediately, working -- doing what's called crater analysis to find out where it came from, and they concluded it came from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did General MacKenzie leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General MacKenzie left, to the best of my knowledge, in about July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, then, I take it from your response to Judge Robinson that you gave no credence to any stories you might have heard to that effect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is right, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just make one very quick follow-up before we take the break. Because I thought you said you had been the target of a government sniper at one time, so why would government forces be interested in sniping at the -- at the -- at journalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was within Bosnian Serb-held territory, I was close to an active front line, and I see no reason why -- I never felt the journalists as journalists were targeted from start to finish, but I was rather unwisely in the open and there was a lot of led flying about and one of these bullets nearly killed me, and, Your Honour if I may say so, this happens to you, you tend to take things personally. They tend to think that -- that I could have just been unlucky to have been so close to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But suppose you had been just an ordinary civilian. You would have been living in -- sorry. Oh, you said you were living in Bosnian Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this -- the date of that incident, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was the morning of the big battle for the hotel grounds, which I think was the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the pictures that we saw of the incident on the Markale, are these pictures yours? Did you shoot them yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are a mixture, Your Honour, of pictures shot by my own cameraman and some that came from the Sarajevo agency pool, but they were predominantly shot by my own cameraman, because the Sarajevo pictures were too vivid for me to be allowed to use, allowed by the BBC, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank Judge Mindua for asking that. You should have led evidence on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I assume from the question and Mr. Bell's answer that he's referring to his own report, the first one, P622, when he talks about whose cameraman shot the images.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your cameraman, Witness, got there to this spot right after, I surmise, right after the incident happened? I'm looking at the scene as it looks on the pictures. There's a crowd. There's a lot of cars. There's a lot of traffic. This cameraman of yours, was he already there when it happened or did he get there a while later, and in that case, how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second set of pictures that you saw were obviously shot by a cameraman who was almost on the spot when it happened. Towards the end of that sequence you will see some white armoured civilian armoured vehicles which were the press vehicles which came down as fast as possible from the press briefing at the United Nations where we all there. Therefore, I would guess that between the second more vivid coverage you saw and the first coverage, there was probably a time-lapse of about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And are you now finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you are to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic and I am a lawyer from the Paris bar. I defend Mr. -- I defended General Dragomir Milosevic, and I will now ask you a few questions regarding your statement of today. And I will also refer to your statement that you gave to the Prosecutor on the 29th of December, 1995, and I will also be referring to the statement of the 1996 -- February of 1996. Do you recall giving those statements to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Tonight, we're not going to have much time, so I will start with the statements in question. It's document bearing number DD00-20085.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction. DD00-20085.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Your document is -- what is the date of your document?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Three dates: We have the 29th of December of 1995 and 6th and 7th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I imagine that you yourself or maybe you went somewhere or maybe you had people come over to see you to take this statement. Do you recall giving this statement on those three dates -- these three statements?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or start over. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall giving these statements on these dates?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I recall certainly at one point two lawyers from the Tribunal came to my home in north London and we did it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So it was on three different occasions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It looks as if two of the dates were consecutive, so I think we could take them really to have been two different sessions. I can't remember if one of them was by telephone or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, I would like you to take a look at the screen and to tell us if this statement is bearing your signature, if the left-hand page bears your signature. Can you confirm that to us?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this statement covers the entire period during which you were in Bosnia, in Croatia, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The period that we are interested in is Sarajevo, between the 10th of August, 1994, and the 21st of November, 1995. This is why I would invite everybody to go to page 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is that in English; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm going to give the reference in English because my statement [as interpreted] is in English, and I imagine that in B/C/S there is also a page that we can find easily. It must be the same page, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on that page, on two or three places there is a mention of a name, Milosevic. Could you please confirm to us that the mention here is not Dragomir Milosevic but Slobodan -- is not Slobodan Milosevic, but, rather, Dragomir Milosevic. I'm only asking you this to avoid confusion. Now, I'm interested in the paragraph that begins by, "if there was a general pattern." It's towards the middle of the page. And I would like to you read out loud that paragraph, please. And then we will talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: "If there was a general pattern to the fighting in the Sarajevo during the whole of the siege, it was that the Muslims would attack outwards with small arms and infantry, and the Serbs would respond with artillery because that was their strength. The world therefore got an impression that Sarajevo was under constant and unprovoked bombardment. However, the war was being waged by both sides. I would even say that the Muslims had a political interest in provoking the Serbs to use their heavy artillery."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you maintain what is said here in this portion of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I've -- I wrote a book about the war in Bosnia making some of the same points, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We all have access to internet nowadays. My learned friend, Ms. Edgerton, sent me an article. It seems to be sort of a note that was -- notes that were taken during a televised programme taken with Mr. Mick O'Regan. I don't know if I pronounce his name correctly. Can you confirm that? Do you recall this? It's something to do with a -- with a role that reporter plays before international jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, I don't recognise from your pronunciation the name of the reporter. If could you spell it, maybe. Was it a BBC programme? It doesn't matter, because if I said it, I'll stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There is no problem. I will spell the name for you. His first name is Mick and then there's O-'-R-e-g-a-n.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I honestly don't remember the programme. I do vaguely remember his name. I do a lot of television, ma'am. But I'm probably quite happy to stand by whatever I said. You can try me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So I'm going to quote something that was said during that interview. It was said that the war in Bosnia, amongst other things, was a televised war. Would you be able to confirm this to us? Or do you maintain this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I do. I do. The key qualification is among other things. The war of words and -- and images was -- was extremely important to both sides. It may interest you to know that our -- we were bombed out of our Ilidza headquarters in the second week in May 1992. I had just left, and the -- the editing equipment that we left behind on the video tapes formed the basis of Bosnian Serb television when it was set up in Pale. I only mention this to show how important the televised war was to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So most of the time you were at the Holiday Inn Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: We were in the Hotel Serbia in Ilidza for the first period for about a month. After that, most of the time in Sarajevo, yes, we were in Holiday Inn. But, of course, when we moved to Central Bosnia we were elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly wait for the end of the question, thank you, before answering.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Bell, the interpreter is asking you to wait until the question has been asked so there is no overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe it's better to put your headphones. This is why I put my headphones as well. For the interpreters it's easier if we wait between answers and questions. So, I would like to refer to the period going from the month of August of 1994 up until the end of the Dayton agreement. So could you please confirm to me that the Holiday Inn Hotel was in a way your place of residence while you were in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Correct, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We saw some video clips earlier and we will take a look at more video clips tomorrow, video clips that were taken by yourself. We noticed some incidents, and there was an incident that took place right in front of the Holiday Inn Hotel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I would say more than one of those incidents took place in front of the Holiday Inn Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time, how were you able to find out where the shots were coming from -- when civilians who were targeted in front of the Holiday Inn, how did you know where the shots were coming from? I'm not asking you to give us a name but what was the -- what way, what mean did you have of knowing this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I suppose the answer is common sense. If a French soldier is standing on -- on the protected side of an armoured vehicle and he looks around the corner and there's a -- you hear the shot and he flinches back, he knows where it's coming from, so I think the answer is common sense. In the same way that when I was nearly killed when I was in Ilidza by somebody on the government side, I assume that the shot came from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, precisely, I remember clearly that you said that when you were hit by a bullet in Ilidza, this is what you said: "The confrontation line was active." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I wasn't hit by a bullet, madam. I was nearly hit. Yes, there was a -- there was a battle going on, on the perimeter of the park land some way away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you must have noticed at that time -- fortunately you were not hit. You must have noticed that the line of confrontation, when it's busy, it's a very dangerous spot, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And now, based on your memories which I presume must be reliable of the -- the confrontation line near the Holiday Inn was relatively close?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was close. I mean, I had been on the Bosnian Serb side and their forward positions which were in one of the faculties of the university, and I would have thought, I would guess that was no more than two or at the most 300 metres from the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, which faculty are you talking about, philosophy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I remember -- my recollection is not absolute, but I do remember a certain irony that war was going on and one of the front lines was in the philosophy faculty. I think it was philosophy, but I couldn't be 100 per cent certain after 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you must have seen soldiers of the ABiH around the Holiday Inn, near the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They were not much in evidence there. I did on one occasion see a group who I took to be snipers, because they were -- there were four, five, men in uniform and they had with them encased weapons, which were surely not fishing rods, and they were going into the office building of the -- of the parliament. But in most of the front line -- I mean, the positions could be only 40 metres or so from each other and the soldiers, for their own protection, wouldn't be out where you could see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, we have come to the time when we must adjourn. As indicated earlier, tomorrow we will start at 8.30. The sitting schedule for tomorrow has been sent, I understand, by e-mail to all the parties, and I hope it is satisfactory. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
